title: Oncle Lee Kăo Restaurant Review: Modern Chinese Grill Energy in Montréal

blocks.text: Oncle Lee Kăo feels like the “grown-up little sibling” of Oncle Lee on Laurier: still playful, still crowd-pleasing, but sharper around the edges. More grill smoke, more polish, and a dining room that’s built for nights that feel like a plan. It’s the kind of spot where you can keep it casual (share a few plates and a cocktail), or quietly turn it into a full date-night arc without ever feeling like you’re doing fine dining cosplay.
They’re also listed in the Michelin Guide’s **Bib Gourmand** selection, which fits the whole idea here: high-quality cooking and a great night out without the stiff “special occasion only” vibe.
Oncle Lee Kăo
**Location:** Ville-Marie, Montréal (former Ikanos / Garde-Côte space)
**Price Range:** $$-$$$ (share-plates add up, but it’s easy to control the total)
**Cuisine:** Contemporary Chinese with a “kăo” (grill) focus
**Dress Code:** Casual to Smart Casual
**Quick Verdict:**

items: Best For: Romantic dinners, “let’s try everything” friend nights, business meals that still feel fun
Conversation Friendly: 3.5/5 (lively room, but not chaotic)

blocks.text: The Vibe (Room + Energy)
In the former location of Ikanos and Garde-Côte, Oncle Lee Kăo opened in late January 2025. It immediately made sense as a Montréal “date restaurant” because the room does half the work for you.

The space seats around 80, with soaring ceilings that give it elegance without making it feel cold. The design leans chic and minimalist: lots of wood, burnt-orange leather accents, Chinese artworks, and a few red lantern touches that keep it from feeling too sterile. There’s also a private room in the back (roughly 12–36 people), which makes it a strong group option when you want something nicer than “let’s just do dumplings.”
**Lighting:** Warm + flattering
**Noise Level:** Medium (buzzy, social)
**Best Seats:** A two-top along the edges if you want to stay locked-in; bigger tables if you’re sharing everything
About

Oncle Lee Kăo is the newest project from the team behind Bouillon Bilk, led by chef Andersen Lee alongside chef Émile Collette, front-of-house manager Marie‑Alexandra Dahouet, and restaurateurs Mélanie Blanchette and François Nadon (also behind Bouillon Bilk, Cadet, and Place Carmin).

If the original Oncle Lee on Laurier became a neighborhood staple for comfort-forward Chinese flavors, Kăo is the “different lane” version. It’s more relaxed, more contemporary, and built around “kăo”, the Mandarin word for grill, with a menu that leans into smoky char, crisp textures, and shareable plates that encourage ordering wide.
What to Order (Date-Night Game Plan)
This is a “order in waves” restaurant. You want the table to keep evolving while the conversation stays steady.
**My ideal flow for two:**
1) **Something briny + cold** to wake up your appetite
2) **A veg plate** with real punch (sweet/sour, spice, crunch)
3) **A raw/quick-seared beef or seafood plate** for contrast
4) **One comfort carb** to make the night feel complete
5) **Dessert (even if you think you’re too full)** because the room is built for lingering
**Easy order for two (trust me, 4 dishes is plenty):**

items: Optional: dessert if you still have room

blocks.text: What I Ordered (and how it ate)
Steamed Oysters (black bean)

A strong opener: clean, briny oysters with a savory black bean hit that reads salty-sweet and fermented in the best way. It keeps the oyster feeling *oyster-y* (fresh, ocean, cold) but adds enough depth that it doesn’t disappear in one bite.
Sweet & Sour Eggplant (peanuts, bacon)

This is the plate that makes the table feel alive. The eggplant lands glossy and tender, sweet-and-sour without being sticky-ketchup sweet, with peanuts giving crunch and bacon adding that smoky, salty anchor.
If you like eggplant when it’s jammy and properly seasoned, this is the move. The sweet/sour profile also sets up everything after it. It resets your palate and keeps the meal from feeling heavy.
5 Spice Duck Platter

This is their signature dish, and it totally makes sense once it lands. It’s a big portion of sous vide duck with five spice warmth and a rich, luxurious texture, served platter-style so you can build your own wraps.

It comes with duck rillettes, a ton of cilantro, and a spread of add-ons and sauces so every bite can be different. Think pickled carrot and daikon for crunch and acidity, chili crisp for heat, peanuts, cucumber, a liver mousse, and a hoisin-style sauce.
Beef Tataki (Nordic shrimp, cucumber)

This one tastes familiar in the best way, like hotpot flavors translated into a clean, modern plate. You get that slick chili oil vibe, warm spices, peppers, and a little mala-style tingle, but it still eats light and refreshing with the cucumber and Nordic shrimp.
Garlic Fried Rice
The closer that makes everything feel complete. Garlicky, comforting, and the exact dish you’re grateful for when you realize you ordered like “tasting menu energy” but still want to leave satisfied.
It also works as the “bridge” plate: if one person wants to keep drinking and chatting, fried rice buys you time. It keeps the night going without forcing you into another heavy main.
Drinks (Pandan Express)

I ordered the **Pandan Express** and I loved it. You can really taste the pandan: clean, aromatic, not perfumey. The baiju reads crisp rather than harsh. It’s one of those cocktails that feels “specific” to the restaurant instead of a generic sweet drink with a fancy name.
Dessert (The Gift That Seals the Night)

The restaurant offered a **Yuzu tartelette**, plus **green tea** and a **fruit platter**, and it landed like the perfect soft ending. Yuzu gives you that bright citrus snap that cuts through the savory meal, and green tea is basically the clean reset button that makes you feel human again.
If you’re trying to make the night feel romantic without being corny, this is exactly the vibe: a dessert moment that feels cared-for.
Service + Pacing

The pacing works well for a share-plates night: you can keep the meal moving, but you can also stretch it out. That’s the sweet spot for a date: steady plates, no awkward gaps, but enough breathing room to talk.
The Honest Take (Who This Is For)
Oncle Lee Kăo does a nice job bringing modern technique and a bit of twist to familiar Chinese flavors. The execution was solid, and I wouldn’t complain about portion size.

That said, it wouldn’t be my first choice if you’re someone who already eats at Chinese restaurants often. A lot of the flavor profiles still feel pretty close to what you can get at a typical Chinese restaurant, just with updated technique and a more premium price point.
If I’m being honest, it also doesn’t hit the same comfort spot as that classic “2 a.m. Chinese food” craving. The food leans oily and heavy, which isn’t always what you want in a dating context.

Where it shines is as a **double date** or **group night**. When you’re sharing a spread and trying everything, it’s genuinely fun. And if you’re not very familiar with Chinese food, it’s still a fair, approachable option in a beautiful room.
The Real Cost (So You Can Plan)
This can be a **controlled budget** night or a “we kept ordering” night.
**Per person:** roughly **$60–120+ (CAD)** depending on how many plates + cocktails
**Best way to keep it reasonable:** 3–4 dishes for two + 1 drink each + dessert
**Worth it?** Yes, especially if you value room + vibe as much as the food
Before/After Activities Nearby (Dating Concept)
If you’re already going out, make it a full little night. This is the “dating concept” part.
**Before dinner (pick one):**

items: **Le Mal Nécessaire** (Quartier International): great cocktail energy without feeling like a club.
**The Coldroom** (Old Montréal): dim, classic, and a strong “start the night” bar.
**Old Montréal stroll**: walk around **Place Jacques-Cartier** and the nearby streets to get into that Old Port mood.

blocks.text: **After dinner (pick one):**

items: **Old Port walk**: head toward the waterfront for a slower, post-meal walk.
**Notre-Dame Basilica** area: even just walking around the square and streets nearby feels like a second location.
**One more drink** nearby instead of dessert if you’re already full.

blocks.text: Booking & Timing
**Reservations:** Nice to have, but I wouldn’t stress. When I booked, there were tons of spots available.
**Best time for dates:**
Date Type Fit
**First Date:** 3/5
Not my top pick for a first date. The food leans oily and bold, and it’s not the kind of meal that makes you feel fresh and flirty after.
**Anniversary / Special Date:** 3.5/5
It’s clean and the room is nice. It’s just not the vibe, in my opinion, for celebrating an important milestone.
**Friends night:** 5/5
This is the sweet spot. Go as a group or double date, order a spread, and share everything. It’s way more fun this way than doing a strict two-person dinner.
Bottom Line

Oncle Lee Kăo is a strong Montréal date-night restaurant when you want contemporary Chinese flavors with real grill energy, a beautiful dining room, and food that’s designed for sharing without feeling messy. Go for oysters, get a sweet/sour veg plate, add something delicate (tataki), and don’t skip the fried rice. If they offer you the yuzu tartelette + green tea moment, take it. It’s the kind of small hospitality detail that makes the night feel special.
**Details**

items: **Tip:** Order in waves: cold/briny → sweet/sour veg → delicate protein → comfort carb → dessert
